content: National and subnational priorities and implementation strategies are designed to address the health and well-being challenges, opportunities, and needs of adolescents within their respective countries. These strategies serve as a reference for policymakers and program managers at both national and subnational levels, assisting them in planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating adolescent health and well-being programs. The first edition of the AA-HA. guidance was published in 2017, building on the momentum of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the United Nations Secretary-General’s Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030). The World Health Organization (WHO) developed this guidance in response to a request from the 68th World Health Assembly to create global guidance for accelerated action on adolescent health. The second edition continues to describe a systematic approach to planning and implementing adolescent health and well-being programs, as outlined in the first edition. The first chapter of the guidance highlights the importance of investing in adolescent health and well-being, summarizing global opportunities and threats. Chapters 2 and 3 provide an overview of the current status of adolescent health and well-being worldwide and evidence-based interventions to improve it. The national-level programming process begins with understanding the country’s epidemiological and developmental profile (needs assessment), analyzing existing efforts and stakeholders (landscape analysis), and conducting a consultative process to set national priorities for adolescent health and well-being. For nationally agreed priorities, the guidance outlines programming options and provides an inventory of key implementation strategies for both intersectoral and single-sector actions. It also equips policymakers with tools to design robust monitoring and evaluation (M&E) frameworks to enhance accountability and improve programs. Case studies throughout the document demonstrate the feasibility and implementation of the recommended strategies. The second edition of the AA-HA. guidance incorporates lessons learned from the application of the first edition, provides updated data on health determinants, mortality, morbidity, and well-being, and highlights recent consensus on core indicators for adolescent health and well-being. It integrates significant political and scientific advances since 2017 and incorporates the concept of well-being into the programming process. This edition shifts from a predominantly health-centric perspective to a more holistic understanding of adolescent well-being, including its implications for programming. Adolescence is a critical and formative phase of human development, characterized by distinct physical, cognitive, social, emotional, and sexual development. This period requires special attention in national development policies, programs, and plans. A global consensus on a comprehensive framework for adolescent well-being sets the stage for a new generation of programs that address interconnected protective and risk factors at multiple levels. These programs promote good health, optimal nutrition, education, life skills, employability, social connectedness, positive values, societal contributions, agency, and resilience, while also addressing macro policies that shape safe and supportive environments. Investments in adolescent well-being yield a triple dividend of health and economic benefits for adolescents now, in their future lives, and for the next generation. Coordinated investments in health and education are particularly impactful, offering mutually reinforcing benefits. Achieving the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development is not possible without investing in adolescent health and well-being, as it directly contributes to goals related to poverty, hunger, education, gender equality, water and sanitation, economic growth, climate change, and peaceful societies. The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the global community’s capacity to prioritize health investments and highlighted the critical role of schools in providing nutrition, social protection, mental health support, and other services. This presents a unique opportunity to reinvigorate global commitments to adolescent health, well-being, and children’s rights, and to increase investments in these areas. Globally, adolescents aged 10–19 years make up 16% of the population, or approximately 2 billion individuals. Over the past two decades, adolescent mortality rates have declined, particularly among older adolescent girls (15–19 years). However, progress has been uneven across regions and population groups. In 2019, road injuries were the leading cause of death among adolescent males, while diarrheal diseases and tuberculosis were the leading causes of death among younger and older adolescent females, respectively. Mental health conditions, iron deficiency anemia, skin diseases, and migraines were the primary contributors to the burden of non-fatal diseases among adolescents. Interventions for adolescents should address all levels of the ecological framework, from individual to structural levels. Tailored, adolescent-responsive health services and interventions are essential to meet their specific needs and circumstances. These interventions should be delivered with quality and universal coverage, such as enforcing road traffic laws or implementing policies that reduce the affordability of tobacco, alcohol, and unhealthy foods. Collaboration across sectors through multisectoral or integrated programming is crucial, given the multidimensional nature of adolescent health and well-being. The education sector plays a particularly important role in influencing adolescent behavior, health, and well-being through large-scale, long-term initiatives. National and subnational governments must identify and address adolescent health and well-being programming priorities. This requires explicit, transparent prioritization processes involving all relevant stakeholders. These processes should include needs assessments, landscape analyses of existing programs and resources, and the application of explicit criteria to set priorities. Over time, countries should reassess their priorities and programming to adapt to changing needs and trends in health, education, employment, migration, urbanization, and technological innovation. The most significant gains for adolescent well-being result from multisectoral action. Countries should invest in intersectoral programs to leverage the amplifying effects of joint action while ensuring that single-sector actions address adolescents’ needs. School health programs, for example, are cost-effective and feasible in all settings, delivering significant gains for human capital. Adolescent-responsive health systems are key to achieving universal health care (UHC). Countries may consider establishing adolescent health focal points within ministries of health to champion adolescent health, coordinate attention to their needs, and facilitate multisectoral action. Adolescents’ perspectives and leadership should be institutionalized and actively supported in the design, implementation, and evaluation of health and well-being programs. To ensure sustainability, funding for adolescent health and well-being programs should increasingly rely on domestic resources. Advocacy efforts should focus on making the case for adolescent health investments within national sectoral strategies and budgets. External funding opportunities, such as the Global Financing Facility and the Global Fund, can provide additional resources. Monitoring and evaluation are essential for adolescent health programs. The Global Action for Measurement of Adolescent Health (GAMA) Advisory Group has proposed 47 priority indicators to focus measurement on the most critical issues. Countries should collect and use data on these indicators to monitor progress and evaluate programs. Periodic evaluations should build on routinely collected monitoring data to ensure programs remain effective and responsive to adolescents’ needs.
